title: How to Diagnose a Cylinder Misfire
summary: Mechanic-first diagnostic guide for separating ignition, fuel, air, and mechanical causes behind a cylinder misfire.
symptoms: Rough idle or shake from one cylinder dropping out
Flashing check engine light if the misfire is severe
Fuel smell from the exhaust in active misfire conditions
Noticeable power loss tied to one cylinder or a shared misfire pattern
diagnostic_logic: Start by separating a single-cylinder misfire from a shared misfire affecting multiple cylinders.
If the code is cylinder-specific, confirm whether the fault follows the plug or coil before moving to injector or compression testing.
If the code is P0300 or multiple cylinders are involved, shared ignition, fuel-delivery, airflow, or timing issues matter more than a single bad part guess.
likely_causes: Weak ignition coil or damaged coil boot
Vacuum leak near one intake runner or across the intake
Low compression, valve-sealing problem, or other mechanical fault
testing_approach: Confirm which code or cylinder pattern is active and whether the misfire is present at idle, under load, or both.
Use swap testing on the spark plug or ignition coil when the fault is isolated to one cylinder.
Inspect the suspect plug for wear, gap, oil intrusion, or fuel fouling before condemning the injector.
Verify injector operation and connector condition if the misfire stays on the same cylinder after ignition checks.
Move to compression or leak-down testing if the misfire does not follow ignition parts and stays fixed on one cylinder.
tools_required: Scan tool with misfire counters and fuel-trim data
Basic hand tools for plug and coil access
Spark tester or known-good ignition part for swap testing
Fuel injector listening or control test method
Compression or leak-down test equipment when needed
pro_tips: A flashing MIL raises catalyst-damage risk, so active misfires should be diagnosed quickly.
Cylinder-specific misfires are usually faster to narrow down than random shared misfires.
Fuel trim behavior helps show whether unmetered air is pushing the misfire path.
common_mistakes: Replacing the injector before checking whether the misfire follows the plug or coil
Ignoring fuel trims and intake leaks when multiple cylinders are involved
Condemning ignition parts without checking plug well oil intrusion or boot damage
Skipping compression testing when the same cylinder keeps misfiring after swap tests

recommended_repairs.title: Spark Plug Replacement Cost
recommended_repairs.description: A strong first repair path when plug condition or swap testing points to worn or fouled plugs.

recommended_repairs.title: Ignition Coil Replacement Cost
recommended_repairs.description: Use this path when the misfire follows the coil or ignition output is clearly weak.

recommended_repairs.title: Fuel Injector Replacement Cost
recommended_repairs.description: Relevant when the fault stays on one cylinder after ignition checks and injector testing confirms the fuel side.

recommended_repairs.title: Intake Manifold Gasket Replacement Cost
recommended_repairs.description: Worth checking when runner-area leak testing shows unmetered air is causing the misfire.

diagnostic_context.intro: Cylinder misfire diagnosis usually starts from rough idle, hesitation, shaking under acceleration, or a flashing check engine light.
